A shop app loads its catalog as one big JSON response. The developer made every step

function and the caller awaits it, the UI stays free.

It's a reasonable guess. In languages such as C# or Kotlin, asynchronous code often does end up on other threads, through a thread pool or a dispatcher. And in Dart, part of it really is true: while a network request or a file read is in flight, your app keeps drawing frames and handling taps. So
looks like "runs in the background". The waiting does happen elsewhere. Your Dart code doesn't.
One isolate, one thread, one event loop

. The Dart docs describe it as being like a thread or a process, except that each isolate has its own memory and a single thread running an event loop. By default, a Flutter app does all of its work on one of them, the main isolate.
The event loop takes events from a queue and processes them one at a time, in order: a tap, a timer, a response that arrived, the rest of an
function. Flutter adds its own events to that queue: on a 60 Hz device, a "paint frame" event 60 times per second. If one event takes too long, the frame events behind it wait, and the user sees
An async function runs synchronously until its first await
doesn't start anything new. The Dart docs put it plainly: an
function runs synchronously until the first
runs its first line right away, on the caller's stack. The
suspends the function and returns a
to the caller, which carries on. When the awaited future completes, the rest of
is scheduled to run later, on the same event loop. At no point does a second thread appear.

When you await an HTTP call or a file read, the platform does the actual I/O outside your Dart code. Meanwhile the event loop is free, so frames and taps keep being processed. That's the half of the belief that holds.
Once the response arrives, though, whatever you do with it is ordinary synchronous Dart:
, sorting 50,000 items, filtering a big list, resizing an image. It runs on the event loop, and while it runs, nothing else does. No frame, no tap handler, no timer. Wrapping it in
doesn't help either: that constructor runs the computation later through
, on the same isolate. It changes when the work runs, not where.
Isolates: a second event loop with its own memory
Real parallelism in Dart means a second isolate. Isolates share no memory and talk only through messages, so values you send are copied (immutable ones like strings are shared).
does the whole round trip for you: it spawns a worker isolate, runs your function there, returns the result to the main isolate and shuts the worker down. The result comes back through
, which hands it over without copying it.

content.text: Measure it and the difference is plain. With a generated 15.8 MB response of 200,000 products, the first version decoded in about 190 ms, and a 16 ms timer standing in for frames didn't fire once in that time. That's more than ten frames at 60 Hz. The
, the whole call took longer, about 290 to 340 ms including starting the worker, but the timer kept firing as often as it did with the app idle.
That's the honest trade-off: an isolate doesn't make work cheaper. It costs a spawn and a copy of what you send, and in return the main isolate keeps producing frames.

Run the app in profile mode and open the DevTools Performance view, which marks frames slower than about 16 ms (on a 60 Hz screen) with a red overlay. Look at which Dart code ran in those frames. Small payloads rarely need an isolate.
